transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2027-09-12
Start: 15:56 UTC
Duration: 52 minutes
Location: Zoom
Attendees: Sarah Kim (Redwood AE), Rajesh Patel (Redwood SE), Lena Ortiz (Redwood SE), Avery Lin (Meridian Head of ML Ops), Marcus Hale (Meridian CTO), Priya Rao (Meridian Platform Eng), Diane Wu (Meridian Procurement), Speaker 6 (intern)

Summary: quick intro, scope of dedicated capacity, hybrid/prewarm ideas, security/compliance checklist, procurement cadence and next steps.

---
[00:00] Sarah Kim: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. quick intros, i'll let meridian folks introduce then we'll jump into what you guys are seeing today.
[00:18] Avery Lin: hi all, avery here, head of ml ops at meridian, we run most models in-house but evaluating dedicated capacity because of bursty inference across our product. main use case is chat+summaries for clinical notes, so data residency and encryption are huge.
[00:42] Marcus Hale: marcus, cto — short timeline, we want a POC in the next 4 weeks-ish, procurement may add time tho.
[00:50] Priya Rao: priya, platform eng, i'll be owning the network side — V P C, peering, firewall rules.
[00:56] Diane Wu: diane from procurement, i'll track contract approvals.
[01:02] Sarah Kim: great, thanks. rajesh and lena from our infra team will cover technicals then i'll follow with pricing and next steps.

[01:20] Rajesh Patel: high level — redwood dedicated is a reserved gpu pool that you can provision in a region or on a private deployment. for your burst pattern the typical approach is a small hot-pool to keep models warm and then a reserved capacity floor. when bursts occur we can either scale within the reserved pool or fallback to hosted api for overflow.
[01:46] Priya Rao: when you say fallback to hosted, is that automatic? how do we handle p i i or PHI?
[01:54] Rajesh Patel: good question — fallback is policy-driven. you can configure routing rules to never send certain traffic to hosted. for example percipient PHI payloads can be blocked from leaving your VPC or require encryption with BYOK. we also support V P C only Dedicated (private control plane) so no data crosses our hosted plane if you need that.
[02:20] Marcus Hale: so what about tenant isolation — we want stronger guarantee than just namespacing, ideally GPU-level fencing between business units.
[02:29] Lena Ortiz: we understand, meridian. we support multiple tenancy topologies. you can do strict node isolation where GPUs are pinned to a tenant, effectively single-tenant nodes, or soft-tenant fencing using cgroups/containers with runtime-level enforcement. single-tenant nodes are the recommended pattern for high-compliance customers.
[02:48] Avery Lin: cost-wise single-tenant nodes are more expensive; do you have guidance on tradeoffs?
[02:55] Rajesh Patel: yes it's a tradeoff — we provide unit economics examples. single-tenant avoids noisy neighbor risk and KV cache contamination, but costs scale with reserved nodes. hybrid approach: pin critical tenants to isolated nodes and put lower-sensitivity traffic on shared pools with strict RBAC and monitoring.
[03:16] Priya Rao: can you explain the kv cache thing — we've seen references to kay vee cache being shared.
[03:22] Rajesh Patel: sure — the KV cache holds activations for autoregressive decoding. by default caches are per-inference session. we avoid cross-tenant cache sharing, but on shared pools the disk-backed prefix cache could be reused if misconfigured; we treat it as per-tenant by default and enforce evictions on tenant switch.
[03:41] Marcus Hale: about hot-pool sizing — our traffic is 80% small messages but with sudden spikes 10x for 30-90 seconds. what's the expected cold start if pool is zero?
[03:50] Lena Ortiz: cold start varies by model size and quantization. for a medium LLM at 8k context, cold start token latency ramp could be 600-900ms one-off, vs hot-pool warm nodes in sub-200ms for small responses. with quantized 4-bit kernels you can shave latency but need compatibility testing.
[04:12] Avery Lin: do you support automatic prewarm policies? we don't want to manage pools manually.
[04:18] Rajesh Patel: yes, we have autoscale and prewarm policies. examples: keep N prewarmed instances per region or maintain a CPU/GPU utilization threshold. you can also schedule prewarms for predictable bursts (cron). there's also a 'fast-burst' policy that maintains a tiny prewarm plus burst to hosted for overflow.
[04:38] Priya Rao: network egress — are there specific firewall ports/outbound endpoints we need to allow for dedicated?
[04:45] Lena Ortiz: for VPC Dedicated you'll open peering and have a few egress ip ranges to allow for control-plane telemetry and image pulls. we'll send a concrete network diagram — include CIDR + port list.
[04:58] Marcus Hale: on encryption — BYOK and H S M supported? key rotation?
[05:03] Rajesh Patel: yes BYOK via K M S integrations, and we have an H S M option for Private. keys can live in your cloud K M S; Redwood supports envelope encryption so model artifacts and traffic can be encrypted at rest and in transit. we'll share the K M S integration guide.
[05:21] Avery Lin: what about audit logs? retention? we might need 1 year of detailed audit for compliance.
[05:27] Sarah Kim: we provide audit logs (API calls, model loads, auth events). retention tiers are configurable; enterprise add-on gives long-term retention and export to S3 or your SIEM.
[05:39] Diane Wu: procurement — expected contract length and SLAs? we need an SLA for uptime and latency percentiles.
[05:46] Sarah Kim: Dedicated comes with SLA options; standard is 99.5% uptime, enterprise SLA negotiable. latency SLOs are workload dependent; we can commit to availability and provide playbooks for failover.
[05:58] Marcus Hale: curious about cost — any rough $/token or $/hour numbers for reserved nodes vs hosted?
[06:05] Sarah Kim: we'll share a pricing sheet. ballpark: reserved nodes are priced monthly with committed usage — per-token economics depend on batching and cache hit rates — we included typical examples in the deck.

[06:30] [--- 6 minute mark, moving to deeper questions ---]
[06:32] Priya Rao: on the technical deep dive — we want Rajesh's team to see our benchmark scenarios: 1) short chat (avg 60 tokens), 2) long summarization (avg 700 tokens), and peak concurrency pattern up to 400 qps for 30-90s. can redwood simulate that?
[06:50] Rajesh Patel: yes we can simulate. recommended first step is a 48h smoke with synthetic traffic to validate latency p99 and cost. if you want exact parity we can also run your workload under NDA.
[07:05] Avery Lin: NDA is fine. if we do a 48h run what's the estimated compute footprint?
[07:11] Lena Ortiz: depends on model size; rough calc: for 400 qps short chat our warm steady state might need ~6 A100-equivalent slots, with peak prewarm to 12 for spikes. we'll give a sizing table.
[07:26] Marcus Hale: A100 equivalent — we actually want Ampere hardware; do you support different GPU types and can we specify hardware?
[07:34] Rajesh Patel: yes, we support different instance types across Dedicated pools. you can pick Ampere or NV GPUs depending on latency and throughput tradeoffs. we can run benchmarked profiles per hardware.

[07:52] [08:00] Marcus Hale: fallback question again — if a request is routed to hosted during overflow how is data handled? logs, retention, encryption?
[08:08] Rajesh Patel: by default hosted will process, but we recommend explicit policy: either never fallback (reject requests), fallback with sanitized payload, or fallback with encrypted payloads using your BYOK. logs for those requests are captured, and you can opt out from storing payloads in hosted logs.
[08:26] Priya Rao: what about geographic residency? EU data must never leave eu-central. can we limit fallback to same region?
[08:34] Lena Ortiz: yes region policy is configurable; fallback routing can be region-aware and we can disallow host fallback outside a geo. for strict residency you'd typically choose Redwood Private or Dedicated with region pinning.

[08:52] [09:00] Avery Lin: security questionnaire — we have standard SOC2/ISO questions, do you have completed reports?
[09:06] Sarah Kim: we have SOC2 Type II for hosted and enterprise customers; for Private we provide deployment guidance and compliance artifacts. we'll share our security pack link during follow-up.

[09:24] [09:30] Marcus Hale: performance tuning — what's the role of quantization? we saw some regressions in quality at 4-bit.
[09:36] Rajesh Patel: quantization is workload-dependent. we offer recommended quantization profiles with evaluation scripts. 4-bit int quant can reduce memory and speed up kernels but sometimes needs calibration to maintain quality. Redwood Optimize has suggestions and can run ablation on your eval sets.
[09:55] Priya Rao: is runtime A/B rollouts supported? we want canary traffic to a new model variant and automatic rollback.
[10:01] Lena Ortiz: yes rollouts, canaries and automatic fallback are in the control plane. you can route a % of traffic by route/model and have automatic fallback to previous model on error or latency regression.

[10:18] [10:30] Diane Wu: rough procurement timeline — we usually take 6-8 weeks but need to align on PII processing terms. do you have a standard DPA?
[10:26] Sarah Kim: yes DPA standard, but for PHI we often do a tailored annex. we'll include the DPA and example contract language in the docs bundle.

[10:40] [11:00] Avery Lin: one more: how do you instrument costs per token across routes? we want per-team cost breakdowns.
[11:08] Sarah Kim: Redwood Console gives token-level cost and latency breakdowns per API key/route/model. you can tag keys for teams to provide chargeback.

[11:22] [11:40] Rajesh Patel: i want to call out a couple implementation pitfalls we've seen: 1) underestimating prewarm needed for long-context models, 2) not accounting for KV cache reuse costs, 3) firewall rules blocking control-plane healthchecks leading to nodes drifting.
[11:44] Priya Rao: noted. we'll be careful.

[12:00] [12:15] Marcus Hale: any references or case studies for regulated healthcare customers?
[12:20] Sarah Kim: yes — we have a couple redacted references; i'll share 1-pager and a contact that did a Dedicated + VPC deployment last year.

[12:35] [13:00] 
[13:10] Alice (Speaker 6): small note, someone asked about prewarming costs being charged even when idle?
[13:16] Sarah Kim: yes reserved nodes are billed on the commit even if idle; hot-pool prewarm is part of the reserved capacity unless you choose burst-to-hosted which is billed per-usage.

[13:40] [14:00] Priya Rao: do you have RBAC integration for our SSO? we use Okta and SCIM provisioning.
[14:06] Lena Ortiz: yes S S O via SAML/OIDC and SCIM for user provisioning. roles map to Console RBAC.

[14:20] [15:00] Avery Lin: technical deep dive — can we get Rajesh's team to propose hot-pool numbers based on our 400 qps and 10x spikes, and include expected cost delta vs host fallback?
[15:09] Rajesh Patel: yes, that's on our action list. we'll model 3 scenarios: minimal prewarm (cost optimized), balanced prewarm (latency vs cost), full-isolation prewarm (latency prioritized).

[15:30] [16:00] Marcus Hale: about failure modes — if a whole rack fails, what's the cross-region fallback pattern?
[16:07] Lena Ortiz: we support multi-region failover and cross-region replication of model artifacts. policy can route traffic to a secondary region; cold-start penalties apply. multi-region Dedicated is more costly but recommended for critical SLOs.

[16:26] [17:00] Diane Wu: timeline recap — you said you'll send pricing and security docs by next week?
[17:32] Sarah Kim: yes i'll send pricing + security pack by 2027-09-15.

[17:45] [18:00] Priya Rao: any blockers from our side before deep dive? we need to prepare network diagram, firewall rules, and a representative eval dataset.
[18:02] Avery Lin: we'll prepare those items.

[18:20] [19:00] Rajesh Patel: quick note on benchmarks — we'll provide example scripts and a spreadsheet template to capture p50/p95/p99 and cost per 1000 requests.

[19:35] [21:00] 
[21:10] Marcus Hale: i also want to flag a budget constraint — we have a cap for first quarter POC; we'd prefer a 6-month reserved rate if possible.
[21:18] Sarah Kim: understood, we'll include term options (6/12/24) and discounts — we'll propose a 6-month starter commitment with the option to extend.

[21:40] [23:00] Lisa (Priya, mislabelled as Lisa): just confirming that network egress IPs will be provided.
[23:06] Lena Ortiz: yes we'll send egress ranges and required CIDR.

[23:30] [25:00] Avery Lin: any red flags we should know about?
[25:05] Rajesh Patel: only that for strict residency and PHI we recommend Dedicated with node isolation or Private deployment; the hosted fallback is convenient but adds compliance considerations.

[25:25] [27:00] 
[27:10] Diane Wu: procurement question — do you require SOC2 attestation to sign?
[27:16] Sarah Kim: not always required but many enterprise customers ask for SOC2. we have that and will share the report under NDA.

[27:40] [30:00] 
[30:12] Rajesh Patel: quick follow: we'll draft a recommended hot-pool sizing doc and sample pricing scenarios (cost vs latency) and will send as an attachment.

[30:30] Marcus Hale: good. if the POC shows promise, we will ask legal to start contract review.

[30:48] [32:00] 
[32:10] Sarah Kim: wrap-up: recap next steps — pricing + security docs by 9/15, VPC diagram from Priya by 9/17, technical deep dive week of 9/20, 48h smoke test targeted 9/27. any other asks?
[32:28] Priya Rao: none from infra.
[32:31] Avery Lin: no. thanks everyone.

[32:36] [33:00] 
[33:10] Diane Wu: i'll coordinate procurement timeline and loop legal.
[33:17] Sarah Kim: perfect. we'll follow up in email, attach the deck and benchmark template.

[33:30] [33:45] 
[33:50] Rajesh Patel: just one last note — if you decide on Ampere we might recommend a slightly different prewarm strategy due to memory/throughput tradeoffs. we'll include hardware-specific guidance.

[34:06] Marcus Hale: ok thanks.
[34:10] [34:30] 
[34:50] Sarah Kim: thanks all — i'll send the notes and action items after this call. talk soon.
[35:00] Meeting ended.

References & links mentioned: deck (link shared after meeting), network diagram template (to be shared), benchmark spreadsheet (to be shared), security pack (SOC2).

Notes about transcription quality: occasional mis-attributions and acronym spacing (S S O, K M S) — speaker 6 may have mislabelled two lines.
